t: LeetCode 1839 — Longest Substring Of All Vowels in Order
o:
## Understanding the problem

A substring is beautiful if it contains every vowel a, e, i, o, u at least once and its letters never decrease alphabetically (all a's first, then all e's, and so on). Given a word consisting only of vowels (length up to 5·10^5), return the length of the longest beautiful substring, or 0 if none exists.

**Example walkthrough:** In "aeiaaioaaaaeiiiiouuuooaauuaeiu", the stretch "aaaaeiiiiouuu" is non-decreasing and uses all five vowels — length 13. In "aeeeiiiioooauuuaeiou", an early run breaks when o drops to a; later, the trailing "aeiou" is beautiful with length 5. A single character like "a" can never contain five distinct vowels, so the answer is 0.

Because any descent kills validity, candidate substrings are exactly maximal non-decreasing runs — so one linear scan that tracks each run's length and distinct-vowel count suffices; anything super-linear risks the 5·10^5 limit.
k: A beautiful substring is a maximal stretch where every character is >= the previous one; it qualifies iff it contains exactly 5 distinct vowels.
Inside a valid stretch, word[i] == word[i-1] repeats a vowel while word[i] > word[i-1] introduces a new one — so a single distinct counter tracks progress.
Any descent (word[i] < word[i-1]) ends the current run and restarts both counters.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute-force expansion from every start
a.i: Try every start index, extend while characters keep rising or staying equal, and check whether the window covered all five vowels using a small set. This restates the definition directly but degenerates to quadratic time on inputs like a long block of a's.
s: For each start i, grow j while j == i or word[j] >= word[j-1].
Track the set of vowels inside word[i..j).
Whenever the set reaches size 5, update the best length with j - i.
a.t: O(n^2) worst case — each start may scan to the string's end (e.g., all a's); too slow at n = 5·10^5.
a.sp: O(1) — the vowel set never exceeds 5 entries.

a.i: One scan suffices: keep the current run's length and how many distinct vowels it contains. While the sequence is non-decreasing, extend the run — bumping distinct whenever the letter strictly increases — and on any descent restart both counters. Whenever distinct hits 5, the whole run qualifies, so record its length.
s: Start with length = distinct = 1 for the first character.
For each i >= 1: if word[i] >= word[i-1], increment length, and increment distinct when word[i] > word[i-1].
After processing index i, if distinct == 5 update best with length.
Return best (0 if no qualifying run appeared).
a.t: O(n) — every character is examined exactly once.
a.sp: O(1) — two integer counters regardless of input size.

w:
## Wrap-up

Present the one-pass version directly; mention brute force only to motivate it. **Common pitfalls:** treating equal adjacent letters as a new distinct vowel (only strict increases count), resetting mid-run on equal characters, or updating the answer before checking distinct == 5 — which would report incomplete runs like aaaeeeooouuu. Strings of length 1 and runs missing an interior vowel correctly yield 0.

**Likely follow-ups:** return the substring itself rather than its length, generalize to k distinct vowels in alphabetical order, normalize mixed-case input, or adapt the run-tracking idea to counting beautiful substrings.
